$comment: Events in 2026 that changed where Flock cameras operate, who pays for them or how their data is kept, as reported in the sources on this site. Kinds: added (new, renewed or kept contracts), ended (cameras switched off or removed), restricted (a law or order limiting use, funding or placement), flock (the company's own changes). Dates are those the sources give; precision says whether the day is known.
rule: Selection: decisions in 2026 by a state, by Flock, or by a city or county council, as reported in the sources on this site, chosen to include contracts added and kept as well as those ended. Not a complete list.

events.text: A new law requires deletion after 21 days unless the data is needed as evidence, limits use to felonies and gross misdemeanors and bars most sharing.
The council votes 5 to 4 to keep the town’s cameras, off since February, switched off.
The council extends the city’s contract for six months, with no sharing with outside agencies and a public transparency portal.
The council votes 6 to 4 for a five-year, $2.1 million contract.
WJAR reports that the State Police will install 39 plate readers statewide under a $597,000 Flock contract signed earlier in the year.
Makes seven days the default for keeping reads for new customers, down from 30; existing customers keep their settings.
The council votes 5 to 3 for a new Flock contract worth about $270,000.
The governor orders state agencies to pause funding for Flock cameras; a state grant program had helped install at least 3,200.
The transportation department revokes permits for cameras on state road rights of way.
The Department of Public Safety says it will keep using its more than 900 cameras but pause installing new ones.
At least 14 cities and counties, Dallas and Houston among them, have switched off more than 900 cameras since the funding pause, The Texas Tribune reports.
The city will keep more than 300 grant-funded cameras on after Flock pauses its payments for 90 days, The Texas Tribune reports.
